issues.legal_issue: The right of pre-emption between co-sharers does not infringe the constitutional right to acquire, hold and dispose of property.
material_facts: A co-sharer sought to pre-empt the sale of the other co-sharer’s share of the property.
The purchasers challenged the application of the right of pre-emption as an infringement of their constitutional property right.
issues.conclusion: The law of pre-emption as between co-sharers does not infringe the constitutional right to acquire, hold and dispose of property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Bhau Ram v. Baij Nath, which held that pre-emption vis-à-vis co-sharers is not an unreasonable restriction on the constitutional right to acquire, hold and dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f). It rejected the proposed distinction between related and unrelated co-sharers, reasoning that an “outsider” means a person who is not already a co-sharer. Nuri Mian v. Ambica Singh was cited for the proposition that the right must subsist at relevant stages, but the Court expressly left open the constitutional argument concerning when a restriction becomes final.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preemption: A party in the proceeding challenged the application of a right of pre-emption as an infringement of the constitutional property right.
predicates.co_sharer_relationship: The claimed right of pre-emption arose between co-sharers of the property.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns pre-emption between co-sharers, the output is that the right does not infringe the property right.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer cannot enforce pre-emption over a sale of leasehold land and the house standing on it when the claimant cannot be substituted for the entire bargain.
material_facts: The claimant already owned a share of the property and sought to pre-empt the sale of the remaining share.
The sale included a house and other buildings standing on rent-paying land held on a subordinate, leasehold tenure.
The claimant sought pre-emption of the property sold, while the land interest was not itself subject to pre-emption under the applicable law.

The house could not be separated from the land for the claimed pre-emption without leaving the claimant unable to take the entire bargain; separated from the land, the superstructure would be movable property.
issues.conclusion: The sale of the leasehold interest was not pre-emptible, and the house standing on that land was not independently pre-emptible; the claimant therefore had no right to pre-empt the sale.
issues.legal_principle: Under the customary application of Muhammadan law, pre-emption is an incident of full ownership and does not attach to property held on a subordinate tenure such as a lease. The claimant must take the entire bargain, and the rule operates reciprocally: the vendor must have been in a position to claim pre-emption of the claimant’s whole bargain if the positions were reversed. A house sold with its foundations may be pre-emptible where the land is itself pre-emptible, but a house on leasehold land cannot be detached from that land to permit partial pre-emption; detached, the superstructure is movable property, which is not subject to pre-emption. The Court relied on Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh for the nature and scope of the right; Gobind Dayal v. Inayatullah, Sakina Bibi v. Amiran, Dashrathlal v. Bai Dhondubai and Shri Audh Behari Singh v. Gajadhar Jaipuria for ownership and reciprocity; and the authorities establishing that leasehold interests are not pre-emptible, including Nathuni Ram v. Gopinath (Full Bench). It agreed with Nathuni Ram’s conclusion that a house on leasehold land cannot be pre-empted separately. The Court also considered the Muhammadan-law texts in Baillie’s Digest and The Hedaya. It rejected the contrary support drawn from Zahur v. Nur Ali because that decision had not addressed the requirement of full ownership in the land, and distinguished Chariter Dusadh v. Bhagwati Pandey because it concerned whether the claimant was a full owner.

rule.if: customary_preemption_claim and co_sharer_claimant and sale_includes_leasehold_land and sale_includes_attached_structure and claim_cannot_cover_entire_bargain

predicates.customary_preemption_claim: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking to enforce a customary right of pre-emption.
predicates.co_sharer_claimant: The claimant relied on ownership of a share in the property as the basis for claiming pre-emption.
predicates.sale_includes_leasehold_land: The transaction sought to be pre-empted includes land held under a subordinate tenure rather than full ownership.
predicates.sale_includes_attached_structure: The transaction includes a house or other structure standing on that land.
predicates.claim_cannot_cover_entire_bargain: The claimant cannot be substituted for the entire transaction, including because the land interest cannot be pre-empted and the structure cannot be treated as a separately pre-emptible property.

issues.definition: When a co-sharer seeks customary pre-emption of a transaction that includes leasehold land and an attached structure, and cannot take the entire bargain, the output is that the pre-emption claim fails.
